sentences.text: Fossils of the genus Nothosaurus have been recovered from former Tethys Ocean regions such as North Africa, Europe, and China.

These reptiles were semi-aquatic, with estimates of their length ranging from about three metres to four metres, and likely moving in the water with webbed toes and a possible tail fin, reminiscent of modern seals.
The species Nothosaurus fortihumeralis is distinguished by a massive humerus whose proximal part is especially robust.
Its humeral shaft narrows to about half the width of the distal end, a unique proportion within the genus.
The dorsal process of the scapula is notably elongated and ends in a relatively sharp tip.
Skin impressions preserve webbed feet, showing adaptation for both swimming and walking on land.
Its broad, flat skull bore long, needle-like teeth specialized for snapping up fish.
The type locality of Nothosaurus fortihumeralis is the Upper Member of the Guanling Formation in Luxi, South China.
The species was described as a new large nothosaurian marine reptile from the Middle Triassic of South China.
Jaw muscles could generate a strong bite to close the mouth, yet they were comparatively weak for reopening it.
Nothosaurus fortihumeralis belongs to the nothosaurid family within the sauropterygian reptiles.
The type species of the genus is N. mirabilis, and the genus comprises nearly a dozen recognized species.
Phylogenetic analysis recovers a monophyletic Nothosaurus, with N. fortihumeralis as the sister taxon to N. jagisteus.
The same analysis collapses the traditional Eusauropterygia, grouping Pachypleurosauria and Nothosauroidea into a single Nothosauriformes clade.
Hanosaurus and Majiashanosaurus are successive sister groups to Nothosauriformes, together forming the monophyletic Nothosauromorpha.
Nothosaurus fortihumeralis lived during the Middle Triassic Anisian age.
The broader genus Nothosaurus existed from the Middle to Late Triassic, approximately 245 to 228 million years ago.
